entries.title: Account merge refused with ACCOUNT_MERGE_SEQNUM_TOO_FAR
entries.why: stellar-core refuses to merge an account whose sequence number is at or above the current ledger's starting sequence number, since the account could be recreated with sequence numbers it already used. The transaction is in the ledger and failed; readers that apply the merge from the envelope remove an account that still exists.

entries.title: BumpSequence below the current sequence number changes only seqLedger and seqTime
entries.why: From Protocol 19 a BumpSequence whose target is lower than the sequence number still succeeds and updates the account's seqLedger and seqTime extension (here adding the extension), while the sequence number stays. Readers that treat a successful bump as a sequence change, or ignore the change, misreport the account.

entries.title: BumpSequence to INT64_MAX, after which the account can never transact again
entries.why: The operation sets the sequence number to 9223372036854775807. Readers that store sequence numbers in a smaller or floating type, or that derive the next sequence by adding one, overflow or round it.

entries.title: ManageSellOffers creating selling and buying liabilities in the account and its trustlines
entries.why: Since CAP-0003 every open offer reserves what it could sell and buy as liabilities: native ones in the account's ext.v1, issued ones in the trustlines' ext.v1. Readers that compute available balance as balance minus reserve, ignoring liabilities, overstate what the account can spend.

entries.title: Protocol 10 upgrade: 50,936 upgrade entry changes add liabilities to accounts and trustlines
entries.why: The Protocol 10 upgrade (CAP-3 liabilities) rewrites the ledger in one go: 50,936 upgrade changes in a 6.47 MB LedgerCloseMeta, giving 2416 accounts and 3935 trustlines an ext.v1 with buying and selling liabilities, updating 10518 offers and removing 7424. Readers that cap meta size, skip upgrade changes, or treat a liabilities extension as a balance change break or mis-account.

entries.title: Transaction bidding 1000 stroops per operation in an uncongested ledger is charged the base fee
entries.why: Since CAP-0005 the fee in the envelope is a maximum bid; in a ledger that is not full stellar-core charges the base fee. Readers that record the envelope fee as paid overstate fees, here tenfold.

entries.title: Fee bump whose inner transaction fails at apply time with txBAD_AUTH
entries.why: The transaction applied first sets AX2's master weight to 0, so the inner transaction, signed by that key alone, fails its signature check while applying. The outer fee source still pays.

entries.title: Fee bump whose inner transaction fails at apply time with txBAD_AUTH_EXTRA
entries.why: As in classic/apply-time-failure-result-codes.bad-auth-extra, an earlier transaction makes one of the inner transaction's signatures unnecessary; inside a fee bump the code lands in the inner result.

entries.title: Fee bump whose inner transaction fails at apply time with txBAD_MIN_SEQ_AGE_OR_GAP
entries.why: The transaction applied first moves GA2's seqLedger to this ledger with a no-op bump, so the inner transaction's min_seq_ledger_gap of 1 is no longer met when it is applied.

entries.title: Fee bump whose inner transaction fails at apply time with txBAD_SEQ
entries.why: The transaction applied first bumps QS's sequence number, so the inner transaction of FB's fee bump meets a stale sequence number. The code sits in InnerTransactionResult, not TransactionResult; readers that read only the outer code see txFEE_BUMP_INNER_FAILED and lose why.

entries.title: Fee bump whose inner transaction begins sponsoring and never ends it: inner txBAD_SPONSORSHIP
entries.why: The inner transaction's only operation begins sponsoring BS2's reserves and nothing ends it, which stellar-core detects after applying the operations; the inner transaction fails with txBAD_SPONSORSHIP inside txFEE_BUMP_INNER_FAILED, and the begun sponsorship is rolled back.

entries.title: Fee bump whose inner transaction fails at apply time with txNO_ACCOUNT
entries.why: The transaction applied first merges NA away; the fee bump that FB pays for NA's transaction then finds no inner source account. Readers that resolve the inner source to attribute the transaction look up an account that no longer exists.

entries.title: Fee bump whose inner path payment failed (over_sendmax): 200 charged of a 2000 bid, inner charged 10
entries.why: The result is txFEE_BUMP_INNER_FAILED wrapping the inner txFAILED[path_payment_strict_receive OVER_SENDMAX]; the outer fee source paid 200 of its 2000 bid and the inner result reports its own fee_charged of 10. Readers that read only the outer arm, take the bid as the fee, or index the failed payment as a movement report wrong values.

entries.title: Fee bump before Protocol 25: G fee source, muxed inner source, inner fee_charged 100 (not zero)
entries.why: Before Protocol 25 the inner result of a fee bump reports a non-zero fee_charged (100 here) beside the outer 200 that the fee source actually paid, and the inner source is a muxed M account. Readers that add the two fees, charge the inner source, or key the source by its M form report wrong fees and accounts.

entries.title: Fee bump with a muxed fee source whose inner payment fails; the inner transaction is charged 0
entries.why: The fee is paid by the base account of an M fee source (ID 7), the inner transaction fails with payment.no_destination and has fee charged 0 from Protocol 25, and the payment's destination was never created. Readers that charge the inner source, store the M form, drop failed fee bumps or record the failed destination misreport the transaction.

entries.title: Soroban fee bump from Protocol 25 on: inner fee_charged is 0 and the fee source pays all
entries.why: From Protocol 25 the inner result of a fee bump reports fee_charged 0: the outer fee source paid everything (443191 debited, 61077 refunded, 382114 charged). Readers that take the inner fee as what the inner source paid, or that attribute the Soroban refund to the inner source, report fees on the wrong account.

entries.title: AllowTrust with authorize = 2 sets AUTHORIZED_TO_MAINTAIN_LIABILITIES
entries.why: Since CAP-0018 AllowTrust's authorize is a flag value, not a boolean: 2 leaves the trustline neither fully authorized nor revoked. Readers that test authorize as true or false call this trustline authorized, or revoked, and both are wrong.

entries.title: First record of a live bucket: METAENTRY carrying the bucket's ledger version (28) and list type LIVE
entries.why: Since Protocol 11 (CAP-20) every bucket starts with a METAENTRY record that states the protocol version the bucket was written under; readers of history-archive buckets must decode it before any ledger entry and use its version to interpret the rest. This one also carries the BucketMetadata ext v1 arm (bucket list type LIVE) that later protocols added for the hot archive. A reader that treats the first record as a ledger entry, or that does not know the ext v1 arm, fails on every live bucket of a current archive.

entries.title: Pubnet transaction with PRECOND_V2 extraSigners: two signed-payload keys and a maxLedger bound
entries.why: The transaction's preconditions name two ed25519 signed-payload signers (P… strkeys with 28-byte payloads) as extraSigners and bound it to ledger 65437036. Readers that cannot decode signed-payload signer keys in preconditions, or that truncate a P… strkey, fail on an ordinary pubnet envelope; readers that index the signers or the failed payment's accounts as participants are wrong.

entries.title: PRECOND_TIME with a lower bound and maxTime 0, meaning no upper bound
entries.why: maxTime 0 means unbounded, not a deadline at the epoch. Readers that compare the close time with maxTime literally report a valid transaction as expired.

entries.title: PRECOND_V2 with ledger bounds, minSeqNum, minSeqAge, minSeqLedgerGap and two extra signers
entries.why: Every PRECOND_V2 field except the time bounds is set: an unbounded maxLedger of 0, a minimum sequence number that lets the sequence number skip one value, a minimum age and gap, and an ed25519 and a signed-payload extra signer. Readers that model only time bounds, or that assume sequence numbers grow by exactly one, lose the preconditions or flag a gap.

entries.title: PRECOND_V2 whose minSeqNum is present and 0, with unbounded time bounds
entries.why: A minSeqNum of 0 is present and lets the transaction apply over any source sequence number below its own; an absent one requires exactly seqNum - 1. Readers and SDKs that test the 64-bit value for truthiness read 0 as absent: they report no minimum-sequence condition, and a transaction rebuilt from the parsed object loses the field and becomes another transaction with another hash.

entries.title: Claimable balance ID derived from the un-muxed source of a muxed-source transaction
entries.why: The balance ID is the hash of the transaction source's base account, the sequence number and the operation index. A reader that hashes the muxed source, or recomputes the ID with another preimage, finds a balance that does not exist.

entries.title: Claim of a balance ID that does not exist fails at apply with DOES_NOT_EXIST
entries.why: stellar-core checks a claimed balance ID only when it applies the operation, so a claim of a balance that never existed reaches the ledger as a failed transaction. Readers that trust the ID in a failed operation look up, or even create, a balance that is not there.

entries.title: Claim predicate nested to the maximum depth of four, for a claimant account that does not exist
entries.why: A predicate may nest AND, OR and NOT four levels deep, and its claimant need not exist. Readers that recurse less deeply, or that resolve the claimant to an account, fail on a balance stellar-core accepted.

entries.title: Claim of a balance whose predicate is NOT(UNCONDITIONAL) fails with CANNOT_CLAIM
entries.why: NOT(UNCONDITIONAL) is a valid predicate that is never true, so the named claimant can never take the balance. A reader that records a claim from the operation instead of the result, or treats the balance as claimable, credits funds that never moved.

entries.title: CreateClaimableBalance with ten claimants, each under a predicate four levels deep
entries.why: Ten claimants is the most claimants<10> holds and four levels the deepest predicate stellar-core accepts. Readers with a smaller claimant column, a recursion limit below four, or that list every claimant as an affected account get this balance wrong.

entries.title: BEFORE_RELATIVE_TIME(INT64_MAX) in the operation, BEFORE_ABSOLUTE_TIME(INT64_MAX) in the ledger entry
entries.why: stellar-core converts a relative predicate to an absolute time when it stores the balance, saturating at INT64_MAX. A reader that shows the operation's predicate as the balance's, or adds the close time itself and overflows, reports a condition the ledger does not hold.

entries.title: PathPaymentStrictSend crossing one offer, with its claim atom in the result
entries.why: A strict-send path payment fixes what is sent; what the destination receives and which offers were crossed are known only from the result. Readers that take the destination amount from dest_min, or the trade from the path, report a payment that did not happen.

entries.title: Last successful pubnet inflation: ten payouts, inflationSeq 278, operation removed in Protocol 12
entries.why: INFLATION was removed in Protocol 12, so only history carries it: one operation credits ten accounts, the payouts listed in the operation result, and the header's inflationSeq advances to 278. Readers built after Protocol 12 may not know the operation or its result arm, and the regenerated lake meta reports the payouts as native mint events that no transaction ever emitted at the time.

entries.title: AccountMerge into a muxed destination: the source account is removed, the base destination credited
entries.why: The merge names an M address with ID 42, but the removed account's balance lands on the base G account and the ID survives only in the classic event's to_muxed_id. Readers that look for an account under the M address, or that model the merge as a payment and keep the source, misreport both sides.

entries.title: Muxed address from ID 2^53+1 passed as a native number: exact or refused
entries.why: 2^53+1 is a valid uint64 but not a safe IEEE-754 double: a JavaScript number literal is already 9007199254740992 before the SDK sees it, so an SDK must encode the exact ID or refuse the number.

entries.title: Muxed address from ID 2^64 (one past the uint64 range) must be refused
entries.why: MuxedAccount.med25519.id is a uint64; a builder that accepts a value no uint64 equals encodes some other ID, and the muxed address then routes to a different sub-account than the caller meant.

entries.title: Muxed address from the largest uint64 ID, 2^64-1, encodes exactly
entries.why: 2^64-1 is the largest valid muxed ID; it exceeds int64 and float precision, so a builder that routes it through a signed or floating type changes it.

entries.title: Muxed address from an empty ID string must be refused
entries.why: MuxedAccount.med25519.id is a uint64; a builder that accepts a value no uint64 equals encodes some other ID, and the muxed address then routes to a different sub-account than the caller meant.

entries.title: Muxed address from the ID string "0x10" must be refused
entries.why: MuxedAccount.med25519.id is a uint64; a builder that accepts a value no uint64 equals encodes some other ID, and the muxed address then routes to a different sub-account than the caller meant.

entries.title: Muxed address from ID -1 must be refused
entries.why: MuxedAccount.med25519.id is a uint64; a builder that accepts a value no uint64 equals encodes some other ID, and the muxed address then routes to a different sub-account than the caller meant.

entries.title: Payment with muxed transaction source, operation source and destination at extreme IDs
entries.why: Muxed IDs live only in the envelope and in event data: the transaction source is muxed with 2^64 - 1, the operation source with 2^63 and the destination with 2^53 + 1, while every ledger entry change is keyed by the base G account. Readers that store the M form instead of the base account, keep IDs in signed 64-bit integers or floats, or attach one source ID to the other lose or corrupt the routing.

entries.title: Path payment whose muxed transaction source has a muxed ID above 2^63
entries.why: The muxed ID 15723465199396777564 does not fit a signed 64-bit integer or a double. Readers that store it as int64 get a negative number, and readers that go through a float lose the low digits, so the muxed identity is silently wrong.

entries.title: Transaction whose source is a muxed account with muxed ID 0
entries.why: Muxed ID 0 is a real ID: the source is the M address of the account with ID 0, not the plain G address. Readers that use 0 as 'no muxed ID' drop the M form, and readers that key on the M form split one account into two.

entries.title: Pre-authorised transaction fails, and its pre-auth-tx signer is removed all the same
entries.why: A pre-auth-tx signer is used up when its transaction is applied, whatever the outcome: here the payment fails, yet the signer disappears from the account in the transaction-level changes, before any operation runs. Readers that take signer changes only from operations, or skip failed transactions, keep a signer that no longer exists.

entries.title: Pubnet ledger 11688015: MANAGE_SELL_OFFER_SELL_NO_ISSUER (Protocol 8)
entries.why: Before Protocol 13 an offer whose selling asset's issuer account did not exist failed with MANAGE_SELL_OFFER_SELL_NO_ISSUER. Protocol 13 (CAP-30) removed the code, so a reader built from the current result codes alone, or a decoder that drops removed codes, cannot read this historical result.

entries.title: Pubnet ledger 16966241: MANAGE_SELL_OFFER_BUY_NO_ISSUER (Protocol 9)
entries.why: Before Protocol 13 an offer whose buying asset's issuer account did not exist failed with MANAGE_SELL_OFFER_BUY_NO_ISSUER. Protocol 13 (CAP-30) removed the code, so a reader built from the current result codes alone cannot read this historical result.

entries.title: Pubnet ledger 25599078: MANAGE_BUY_OFFER_BUY_NO_ISSUER (Protocol 11)
entries.why: ManageBuyOffer existed with NO_ISSUER codes only in Protocols 11 and 12: CAP-30 removed them in Protocol 13. A buy offer whose buying asset's issuer did not exist failed with MANAGE_BUY_OFFER_BUY_NO_ISSUER, a code a reader built from the current definitions alone has never seen.

entries.title: Pubnet ledger 28489743: PATH_PAYMENT_STRICT_SEND_NO_ISSUER with its asset payload (Protocol 12)
entries.why: PathPaymentStrictSend was added in Protocol 12 and its NO_ISSUER code removed in 13 (CAP-30), so the arm exists in ledgers of a single protocol. Like its strict-receive sibling it carries the Asset whose issuer is missing; readers that treat failure arms as void misread it.

entries.title: Pubnet ledger 29385104: MANAGE_BUY_OFFER_SELL_NO_ISSUER (Protocol 12)
entries.why: ManageBuyOffer existed with NO_ISSUER codes only in Protocols 11 and 12: CAP-30 removed them in Protocol 13. A buy offer whose selling asset's issuer did not exist failed with MANAGE_BUY_OFFER_SELL_NO_ISSUER, a code a reader built from the current definitions alone has never seen.

entries.title: PATH_PAYMENT_STRICT_RECEIVE_NO_ISSUER carrying the path asset whose issuer is missing (pubnet, Protocol 8)
entries.why: Before Protocol 13 a path payment through an asset whose issuer account does not exist failed with NO_ISSUER, and that result arm carries the Asset itself, unlike the other failure arms, which are void. A reader that treats every failure arm of PathPaymentStrictReceiveResult as void, or that only knows the codes stellar-core still emits, misreads or rejects the result.

entries.title: Transaction failed with txBAD_SPONSORSHIP: a sponsorship left open at the end of the transaction
entries.why: A transaction that begins sponsoring future reserves and never ends the sponsorship fails as a whole with txBAD_SPONSORSHIP (-14), a transaction-level code with no operation results. Readers that expect every failed transaction to carry operation results, or that map only the common codes, drop or mislabel it.

entries.title: BeginSponsoringFutureReserves by an account that is itself being sponsored fails with RECURSIVE
entries.why: Sponsorship cannot nest: once SA begins sponsoring SB, SB may not begin sponsoring SC in the same transaction. The first and third operations succeed on their own, the second fails, and the whole transaction fails; readers that take per-operation success as final record a sponsorship that was rolled back.

entries.title: Protocol 16 upgrade removes the sponsoring ID from one offer: STATE with ext.v1 sponsor, UPDATED with ext v0
entries.why: The Protocol 16 upgrade on pubnet carries exactly one entry change: offer 289733046 loses its sponsoringID (LedgerEntry ext.v1 → v0) with every other field equal. A reader that ignores upgrade changes keeps a sponsorship that no longer exists; one that diffs only data misses the ext change.

entries.title: RevokeSponsorship of a claimable balance with no new sponsor fails with REVOKE_SPONSORSHIP_ONLY_TRANSFERABLE
entries.why: A claimable balance must always have a sponsor, so its sponsorship can be transferred but never revoked. The failed revoke names the balance in its envelope; readers that apply it report the balance unsponsored.

entries.title: RevokeSponsorship of the middle signer leaves signerSponsoringIDs = [G, null, G]
entries.why: signerSponsoringIDs runs parallel to the signer list and holds null for an unsponsored signer. Revoking the middle signer's sponsorship leaves a null between two sponsor IDs, which readers that compact the array, stop at the first null or assume all-or-nothing sponsorship misalign.

entries.title: Sponsorship sandwich creating an account with a zero balance, a signer and a trustline
entries.why: Every reserve of the new account is carried by the sponsor: it is created with balance 0 and its account, signer and trustline name the sponsor in places outside the entry data (the LedgerEntry extension and signerSponsoringIDs). Readers that ignore those extensions mis-attribute reserves or reject a zero starting balance.

entries.title: First pubnet ledger whose StellarValue is SIGNED, one ledger after the last BASIC one
entries.why: From Protocol 15 on, StellarValue.ext is SIGNED with the node ID and signature of the validator that nominated the value; the upgrade ledger 32747293 still has BASIC and this one, 32747294, is the first SIGNED. Readers that expect one arm for the whole history, or that read the signed fields as part of the close time, mis-decode the header.

entries.title: Ordinary Protocol 28 ledger from a local core: StellarValue in the whole-second SIGNED arm
entries.why: Before Protocol 30 every closed ledger carries STELLAR_VALUE_SIGNED (arm 1) with the validator's key and signature; Protocol 30 replaces it with the millisecond arm. Readers built for one arm must still decode the other, on both real passphrases.

entries.title: txTOO_LATE in a closed ledger (Protocol 13): fee charged, sequence number not consumed, no operation applied
entries.why: Before Protocol 15 (CAP-34) a transaction was checked against the previous ledger's close time when it was nominated and against the new close time when it was applied, so one whose max_time fell between the two was included, charged its fee and then failed with txTOO_LATE without consuming its sequence number. Here max_time is one second before the ledger's close time. Readers that assume a failed transaction always bumps the source's sequence number, that expect operation results on every failed transaction, or that treat txTOO_LATE as a submission error that never reaches a ledger get this transaction wrong.

entries.title: Account flags = 0xF: required, revocable, immutable and clawback enabled at once
entries.why: All four authorization flags can be set in one operation, after which none can change. Readers that store only the flags they know, or only required and revocable, report an issuer that can still be changed or cannot claw back.

entries.title: The same trustline transition by AllowTrust (asset code) and by SetTrustLineFlags (full asset)
entries.why: AllowTrust names an asset by its four-byte code and an authorize value; SetTrustLineFlags names the full asset and flags to clear and to set. Both reach the same trustline state here, and a reader must report the two identically.

entries.title: Claimable balance with ext.v1 flags = 1 (clawback enabled), clawed back in the same transaction
entries.why: A balance made from a clawback-enabled trustline inherits CLAIMABLE_BALANCE_CLAWBACK_ENABLED_FLAG in an ext.v1 the original entry layout does not have, and the issuer can then remove it with ClawbackClaimableBalance. Readers that ignore the extension, or treat every removed balance as claimed by its claimant, credit the wrong account.

entries.title: ClawbackClaimableBalance of a balance without the clawback flag fails with NOT_CLAWBACK_ENABLED
entries.why: Only a claimable balance created from a clawback-enabled trustline can be clawed back; CI issued CBA without AUTH_CLAWBACK_ENABLED. The issuer is right and the balance exists, so only applying the operation reveals the failure; readers that apply the envelope remove a balance that is still claimable.

entries.title: Clawback whose from is a muxed account
entries.why: ClawbackOp.from is a MuxedAccount. The trustline debited and the event both name the base account; readers that key the clawback by the M address, or drop operations whose from is muxed, lose or misplace the movement.

entries.title: AllowTrust revocation that must redeem pool shares inside a sponsorship sandwich whose sponsor lacks reserve fails with LOW_RESERVE
entries.why: The AllowTrust form of the same failure: revoking HL2's LX authorization would redeem its pool shares into claimable balances whose reserves SP, sponsoring HL2 in this transaction, cannot pay. ALLOW_TRUST_LOW_RESERVE exists only for this redemption path.

entries.title: Pool ID of the Go SDK test asset paired with itself must be refused
entries.why: stellar-core's check is a strict assetA < assetB, so a pool of an asset with itself is invalid; a builder that tests <= accepts it and returns the ID of a pool that cannot exist.

entries.title: Pool ID of the Go SDK test pair given in XDR byte order (issuer keys ae7b… < b619…)
entries.why: stellar-core accepts a constant-product pool only with assetA < assetB in XDR byte order (type, code bytes, then the issuer's raw key); readers that order issuers by their strkey text refuse this valid pair, because the two orders disagree here.

entries.title: Pool ID of the Go SDK test pair given in reverse byte order must be refused
entries.why: The pair is in the reverse of stellar-core's XDR byte order; a builder that orders issuers by strkey text accepts it and returns the ID of a pool that cannot exist on the network.

entries.title: Pool ID of a pool whose two assets are the same must be refused
entries.why: stellar-core's check is a strict assetA < assetB, so a pool of an asset with itself is invalid; a builder that tests <= accepts it and returns the ID of a pool that cannot exist.

entries.title: Pool ID of the testnet USD pair given in XDR byte order (issuer keys e305… < f7a4…)
entries.why: stellar-core accepts a constant-product pool only with assetA < assetB in XDR byte order (type, code bytes, then the issuer's raw key); readers that order issuers by their strkey text refuse this valid pair, because the two orders disagree here.

entries.title: Pool ID of the testnet USD pair given in reverse byte order must be refused
entries.why: The pair is in the reverse of stellar-core's XDR byte order; a builder that orders issuers by strkey text accepts it and returns the ID of a pool that cannot exist on the network.

entries.title: Authorization revocation redeems pool shares into two claimable balances (POOL_REVOKE_OP_ID)
entries.why: Revoking a trustline's authorization makes stellar-core withdraw the holder's shares of every pool with that asset, remove the pool-share trustline and put each asset into a new claimable balance whose ID hashes ENVELOPE_TYPE_POOL_REVOKE_OP_ID. Readers that see only a flag change miss the removed trustline, the removed pool and both balances.

entries.title: ChangeTrust to a pool share whose asset trustline is fully deauthorized fails with NOT_AUTH_MAINTAIN_LIABILITIES
entries.why: A pool-share trustline needs each non-native asset trustline to be at least authorized to maintain liabilities. IL took HC's LX authorization away entirely, so the new pool-share trustline fails while applying; readers that create the trustline from the envelope invent a pool participant.

entries.title: Path payment whose claim atoms mix pools and the order book: [LIQUIDITY_POOL, ORDER_BOOK, LIQUIDITY_POOL]
entries.why: A path payment's result lists one claim atom per hop, and since CAP-38 an atom is either an ORDER_BOOK offer or a LIQUIDITY_POOL; this one crosses pool, offer, pool. Readers that assume every atom is an offer (with a seller and offer ID) or every atom a pool mis-decode the trades and the amounts.

entries.title: LiquidityPoolDeposit beyond the pool-share trustline's limit fails with LIQUIDITY_POOL_DEPOSIT_LINE_FULL
entries.why: HF's pool-share trustline allows 1,000 shares, far fewer than a 10 XLM and 10 LX deposit mints. The deposit fails while applying; the limit is on the pool-share trustline, not on an asset trustline, which readers that look only at asset limits cannot explain.

entries.title: LiquidityPoolDeposit with the asset trustline only authorized to maintain liabilities fails with NOT_AUTHORIZED
entries.why: Depositing needs full authorization; HN's LX trustline is only authorized to maintain liabilities, which still allows holding the pool share. The deposit fails while applying and nothing moves into the pool; readers that take the envelope's maximum amounts as moved report a deposit that did not happen.

entries.title: First deposit into a liquidity pool: pool updated, asset trustlines already count the pool
entries.why: A deposit moves both assets from the depositor's trustlines into the pool entry and mints shares onto the pool-share trustline; the asset trustlines carry liquidityPoolUseCount in a v2 extension. Readers that look for the pool's creation here, or drop the trustline extension, misread the pool's first funding.

entries.title: Liquidity-pool trustline whose two issuers sort one way as bytes and the other way as strkey text
entries.why: stellar-core requires the two pool assets in XDR byte order. Readers that compare issuers as strkey text reject this valid transaction, or compute a pool ID for the reversed pair that does not exist.

entries.title: Pool-share ChangeTrust whose assets are in raw-key order, the reverse of their strkey order, on both passphrases
entries.why: stellar-core orders a pool's two assets by their XDR bytes, so of two same-code assets the one whose issuer key is lower comes first even when its strkey sorts later. SDKs that validate the order by comparing strkeys reject a valid operation, and with it the transaction or the whole ledger.

entries.title: Pool-share trustline held by the issuer of one pool asset, with no asset trustline
entries.why: An issuer needs no trustline for its own asset, so its pool-share trustline stands alone and counts two sub-entries. Readers that expect two asset trustlines beside every pool-share trustline, or one sub-entry per trustline, get this account wrong.

entries.title: Limit-only ChangeTrust on a pool-share trustline: the trustline changes, the pool does not
entries.why: Changing the limit of a pool-share trustline touches only the trustline. Readers that treat every ChangeTrust on a pool share as a pool event invent a pool change, and readers that key trustlines by asset code cannot even name this one.

entries.title: LiquidityPoolWithdraw into an LX trustline at its limit fails with LIQUIDITY_POOL_WITHDRAW_LINE_FULL
entries.why: HW lowered its LX limit to its exact balance, so the LX a withdrawal would return has nowhere to go. The withdrawal fails while applying and HW keeps its pool shares; readers that apply the envelope burn shares that still exist.

entries.title: Withdraw every share, then ChangeTrust limit 0: the liquidity pool entry is removed as a side effect
entries.why: No operation deletes a pool: stellar-core removes it when its last pool-share trustline goes. Readers that only record what an operation names never see the pool disappear, or attribute the removal to the wrong operation.

entries.title: SetTrustLineFlags revocation that must redeem pool shares inside a sponsorship sandwich whose sponsor lacks reserve fails with LOW_RESERVE
entries.why: Revoking HL1's LX authorization redeems its pool shares into claimable balances, and because HL1 is being sponsored by SP in this transaction, SP must pay their reserves. SP holds exactly its minimum balance, so the revocation fails while applying with SET_TRUST_LINE_FLAGS_LOW_RESERVE; the sponsorship operations around it succeed on their own and are rolled back.

entries.title: PRECOND_V2 with a signed-payload extra signer and its signature
entries.why: An extra signer is a precondition, not a signer of any account: its key appears only in the envelope and the matching signature carries a XORed hint. Readers that record it as an account signer or as a participant invent a relation that no ledger entry shows.

entries.title: SetOptions adds an ed25519 signed-payload signer to an account
entries.why: A signed-payload signer key is a 32-byte ed25519 key plus a 1 to 64 byte payload, so it does not fit a 32-byte key column or a 56-character address column. Readers that assume every signer is a G address truncate it or halt.

entries.title: SetOptions reweights a signed-payload signer, then removes it, in one transaction
entries.why: The same 64-byte-payload signer changes weight in one operation and disappears in the next. Readers that parse signer keys as 32 bytes, or that look up the removed signer by a truncated key, fail on this path; the wallet-backend indexer halted on it.

entries.title: SetOptions adds signed-payload signers with a 1-byte and a 64-byte payload in one transaction
entries.why: Signed-payload signer keys are 32 key bytes plus a 1 to 64 byte payload, so their P strkeys run from 69 to 165 characters. Readers that assume 32-byte or 56-character signer keys truncate or reject them, and the shortest and longest payloads catch off-by-one padding.

entries.title: Transaction authorised only by a signed-payload signature, with a XORed hint
entries.why: The only signature is an ed25519 signature over the payload, not over the transaction hash, and its hint is the key hint XOR the payload hint, so it matches neither key. Readers that attribute signatures by hint or verify them against the transaction hash mislabel or reject a valid transaction.

entries.title: LedgerCloseMeta whose classic transaction-set component holds two transactions and no base fee
entries.why: TxSetComponentTxsMaybeDiscountedFee.baseFee is optional, and a component without it is consensus-valid: each transaction then pays its own bid. stellar-core's builder always writes one, so no ledger holds the absent state on a non-empty component; readers that unwrap the optional, or derive charged fees from the component instead of the results, are untested against it.

entries.title: LedgerCloseMeta whose classic phase has a component without base fee followed by one with base fee 100
entries.why: A classic phase may hold several components; stellar-core sorts the one without a base fee first. A reader that assumes one component per phase, or one base fee per phase, reads the first component's absent fee as the phase's and loses the second.

entries.title: Surge-priced transaction set: a discounted base fee in the component and one bid left out
entries.why: When more operations are queued than a ledger admits, stellar-core leaves the lowest bids out and charges every included transaction the lowest included per-operation bid, which it records as the component's base fee. Readers that compute fees from the header's base fee or from the bid, or that expect every submitted transaction in the next ledger, get the fees and the ledger contents wrong.

entries.title: Surge-priced classic component: base fee 151 against a header base fee of 100, a 1,000,000-stroop bid charged 151
entries.why: Since CAP-42 the fee a transaction pays is set by its transaction-set component: every transaction in a TXSET_COMP_TXS_MAYBE_DISCOUNTED_FEE component with a base fee pays that base fee per operation, not its bid and not the header's base_fee. In this surge-priced ledger the classic component's base fee is 151 while the header still says 100, and a payment that bid 1,000,000 stroops is charged 151. Readers that report the bid as the fee, or compute it from the header base fee, get every fee in the ledger wrong.

entries.title: Map with byte-string keys 0a and 09 sorts to host order 09, 0a
entries.why: The Soroban host accepts an SCMap only with its keys in ascending host order (discriminant first, then the value: numbers by value, bytes, strings and symbols as byte strings); a map built in another order is refused when it reaches a contract or the host.

entries.title: Map with a symbol key "a" and a string key "b" sorts the string first
entries.why: The Soroban host accepts an SCMap only with its keys in ascending host order (discriminant first, then the value: numbers by value, bytes, strings and symbols as byte strings); a map built in another order is refused when it reaches a contract or the host.

entries.title: Native map with u32 keys {10, 9} converts to an SCMap with keys in host order 9, 10
entries.why: The Soroban host accepts an SCMap only with its keys in ascending host order (discriminant first, then the value: numbers by value, bytes, strings and symbols as byte strings); a map built in another order is refused when it reaches a contract or the host.

entries.title: Successful transaction carrying an unconsumed source-account entry that declares create_contract from a B address
entries.why: The authorization tree is a claim of what may be called, not what was. This entry declares creating a contract from a claimable-balance address, the call never does it, and the transaction succeeds. A reader that derives a deployment, a participant or a state change from the entry, or that cannot parse a B… address in the tree, fabricates facts or halts.

entries.title: Matched four-level authorization tree signed by a custom account contract
entries.why: Every node of a four-level authorization tree (seven invocations) is matched by a require_auth call and the signer's nonce is consumed. Readers that flatten or depth-limit the tree, or that only read the root invocation, lose who authorized the nested calls.

entries.title: Matched four-level authorization tree signed by a classic account
entries.why: Every node of a four-level authorization tree (seven invocations) is matched by a require_auth call and the signer's nonce is consumed. Readers that flatten or depth-limit the tree, or that only read the root invocation, lose who authorized the nested calls.

entries.title: Authorization tree submitted twice for the same address: only the first entry is consumed
entries.why: The transaction carries two complete, valid authorization entries for the same address and tree. The call succeeds on the first; the duplicate is decoded but never used (a replay of it would fail on the nonce). Readers that count authorization entries as signatures double-count.

entries.title: Smart-wallet call authorized by the wallet contract itself: participant known only from its consumed nonce
entries.why: The smart-wallet contract CBBRS7XL… authorizes a call on itself with address credentials; the created nonce entry is the only ledger proof that it authenticated. Readers that derive participants from the envelope add every address in the arguments (the context-rule target CBIELTK6… changed nothing), and readers that ignore nonce entries miss the authorizer role.

entries.title: SAC transfer succeeds with two unmatched address-credential entries of an uninvolved account
entries.why: Authorization entries are matched lazily: an entry no require_auth call matches is never authenticated, its expiration is never checked and no nonce is written. The transfer succeeds although U's entries carry a Void signature, expired at ledger 1, one of them a three-level tree. A reader that turns every address in the auth list into a participant records an account the transaction never touched.

entries.title: Authorized call carrying a second, unused authorization entry for the same address
entries.why: The transaction carries two address credentials for the same account; the host consumes only the first, whose nonce is created. The second entry is decoded but never authenticated. Readers that treat every authorization entry as an authenticated signer overstate who authorized what.

entries.title: Custom-account authorization whose signature is an absent vector; the call traps
entries.why: A custom account's signature is an arbitrary ScVal chosen by the submitter. Here it is an ScVal vector with no value (null); the account contract rejects it and the transaction fails. Readers that expect a signature to be bytes or a map of public keys fail to decode the envelope.

entries.title: Custom-account authorization whose signature is Void; the call traps
entries.why: A custom account's signature is an arbitrary ScVal chosen by the submitter. Here it is Void; the account contract rejects it and the transaction fails. Readers that expect a signature to be bytes or a map of public keys fail to decode the envelope.

entries.title: Matched authorization tree with sibling invocations, multisig classic account
entries.why: The root invocation has several sibling sub-invocations, each matched by a require_auth call. Readers that assume one sub-invocation per level, or cap the number of siblings, lose authorized calls.

entries.title: Matched authorization tree with sibling invocations, classic account
entries.why: The root invocation has several sibling sub-invocations, each matched by a require_auth call. Readers that assume one sub-invocation per level, or cap the number of siblings, lose authorized calls.

entries.title: Contract instance storage holding an entry whose key is a 30-by-30 nested map
entries.why: The contract writes into its instance storage under a key that is itself a large nested value, so the instance entry's storage map has a composite key, not a symbol. Readers that assume storage keys are symbols or short scalars mis-render or reject the instance.

entries.title: Contract function 'err_err' returns an error value and the transaction fails as trapped
entries.why: A contract that returns an error makes the whole transaction fail with INVOKE_HOST_FUNCTION_TRAPPED; the error value itself appears only in diagnostic events. Readers that treat a successful-looking call as applied, or look for the error in the result, get it wrong.

entries.title: Contract function 'err' returns an error value and the transaction fails as trapped
entries.why: A contract that returns an error makes the whole transaction fail with INVOKE_HOST_FUNCTION_TRAPPED; the error value itself appears only in diagnostic events. Readers that treat a successful-looking call as applied, or look for the error in the result, get it wrong.

entries.title: Pubnet contract event with eight topics whose data is an SCV_I32
entries.why: Contract event data is any SCVal; signed 32-bit data is rare next to i128 amounts, and this event also has eight topics of five types with a string, not a symbol, first. Readers that assume a symbol first topic or an amount-like data value misread it.

entries.title: Contract events whose data maps have keys that collide after native conversion
entries.why: An ScMap may hold U32(1), String("1") and Symbol("1") (or Bool(true), U32(1), I32(1)) as distinct keys, ordered by type and then value. Converting to a native map keyed by string or number collapses them. Readers that convert silently lose entries.

entries.title: Contract event with four topics that are not addresses or symbols
entries.why: Four topics is the layout of a Stellar Asset Contract transfer event, but these are U32 values from a contract that is no token. A reader that matches token events by topic count alone misreads it.

entries.title: Non-token contract event whose only topic is the symbol transfer
entries.why: The first topic is `transfer` but there is no from, no to and no amount: the data is a string. A reader that classifies events by their first topic as token transfers must reject this one instead of failing or inventing a movement.

entries.title: Contract event with no topics
entries.why: The host sets no lower bound on an event's topic count. A reader that takes topic 0 as the event name, without checking that a topic exists, fails or misreads this event.

entries.title: LedgerCloseMeta v1 with 2000 evicted keys: 1000 temporary contract-data entries and their 1000 TTLs
entries.why: Eviction is ledger-level, not attributed to any transaction: this ledger's evictedKeys lists 2000 LedgerKeys, 1000 temporary CONTRACT_DATA keys of one contract and their 1000 TTL keys. Readers that look for deletions only in transaction meta keep 1000 dead entries; readers that bound the list size small drop the ledger.

entries.title: Pubnet system event executable_update from a contract that replaces its own Wasm
entries.why: A contract that calls update_current_contract_wasm makes the host publish a SYSTEM contract event, not a CONTRACT one: topics `executable_update`, the old and the new executable as vectors, and an empty vector as data. Readers that only handle contract events, or that expect token-style topics, skip or misparse it.

entries.title: ExtendFootprintTTL of an entry larger than the lowered maximum entry size fails with RESOURCE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED
entries.why: The entry was written under the network's 64 KiB limit; a configuration upgrade then lowered contract_data_entry_size_bytes to 2000. stellar-core checks each extended entry against the current limit while applying, so the extension fails although the declared resources were ample. Readers that treat EXTEND_FOOTPRINT_TTL_RESOURCE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED as a resource-declaration mistake misreport it.

entries.title: ExtendFootprintTTL operation whose meta changes only TTL entries
entries.why: Extending a footprint's time to live changes only TTL entries, keyed by a hash of the data key, with no contract-data change. Readers that expect every Soroban operation to change contract data, or that cannot map a TTL key hash back to its entry, drop or misattribute the change.

entries.title: Failed Soroban transaction (i32 overflow) with diagnostic events and no state change
entries.why: The contract's add(7, 2147483647) overflows and the transaction fails as trapped. Its meta has 23 diagnostic events, no consensus events and no operation changes; only the fee and sequence number move. Readers that index diagnostic events as if they were consensus events record calls and values that never took effect.

entries.title: Failed Soroban swap (resource_limit_exceeded) whose diagnostic events show SAC transfers in successful calls
entries.why: The transaction failed with resource_limit_exceeded, so no ledger entry outside the fee changed and there are no contract events, but its 125 diagnostic events include Stellar Asset Contract transfer events marked in_successful_contract_call=true (the sub-calls returned before the budget ran out). Readers that take movements or participants from diagnostic events record transfers that never happened.

entries.title: Fee-bumped Soroban transaction: the resource-fee refund goes to the fee-bump source
entries.why: In a fee-bumped Soroban transaction the outer fee source pays and is refunded; the inner source pays nothing (inner fee_charged 0) and only its sequence number moves. Readers that credit the refund, or debit the fee, to the inner source get balances wrong.

entries.title: Native Stellar Asset Contract transfer from an account to a contract address
entries.why: The native SAC moves lumens from a G account to a C contract: the account entry's balance drops and a Balance contract-data entry is created in the SAC's storage for the contract. Readers that look for a trustline or account change on the receiving side miss the credit.

entries.title: Contract stores a 30-by-30 nested value in persistent contract data
entries.why: A successful call stores a value that is a vector of 30 vectors of 30 values in one contract-data entry. Readers that store contract-data values in small columns, or flatten nested values, truncate or reject the entry.

entries.title: Contract event whose topic is a 30-by-30 nested value, emitted by a successful call
entries.why: A successful invocation emits a contract event whose first topic is a nested vector of 30 vectors of 30 values. Readers that index topics as short scalars, or cap topic size, truncate or reject the event.

entries.title: Invocation whose return value is a 30-by-30 nested value
entries.why: A successful call returns a vector of 30 vectors of 30 values; the return value sits in the transaction's Soroban meta. Readers that store return values as short scalars, or cap their size, truncate or drop it.

entries.title: Self fee bump whose outer fee (15,705,635,118 stroops) exceeds the uint32 range
entries.why: Since Protocol 23 a fee bump may carry an inclusion fee and resource fee above 2^32-1. The outer fee is an int64 of 15,705,635,118 and the fee charged is 8,705,635,318. Readers that store fees as 32-bit integers overflow.

entries.title: RestoreFootprint operation emitting 'restored' changes for an archived entry and its TTL
entries.why: Restoring an archived entry produces LedgerEntryChange arms of type 'restored' for the data entry and its TTL, an arm older readers do not know. Readers that only handle created, updated, removed and state drop the restoration.

entries.title: Pubnet Soroban call whose return value is an SCV_STRING
entries.why: SorobanTransactionMeta.returnValue can be any SCVal; an SCV_STRING return is bytes, not guaranteed UTF-8, and is rarer than the integer, address and void returns readers are tested on. A reader that maps return values only for the common arms, or decodes strings as text without checking, mishandles it.

entries.title: Pubnet Soroban call whose return value is an SCV_U256 above 2^128
entries.why: An SCV_U256 is four 64-bit limbs; SEP-51 renders it as a decimal string. This return value needs all 255 bits, so a reader that narrows 256-bit integers to 128 bits, or to a float, loses it.

entries.title: CREATE_CONTRACT from an issued asset deploys its Stellar Asset Contract: instance and TTL created
entries.why: Deploying the Stellar Asset Contract of an issued asset is an InvokeHostFunction whose only ledger effect is a created contract instance (executable stellar_asset, with the asset in its storage) and its TTL entry. The issuer is read, not changed. Readers that look for a wasm upload or a constructor event, or that attribute the deploy to the issuer, misreport it.

entries.title: Contract event whose data is SCV_ERROR of type SCE_EVENTS (code SCEC_INVALID_INPUT)
entries.why: SCE_EVENTS (6) is another SCError type absent from every other ledger of the corpus. Readers that switch over the SCError type without a default fail or mislabel it.

entries.title: Contract event whose data is SCV_ERROR of type SCE_OBJECT (code SCEC_INDEX_BOUNDS)
entries.why: SCError has ten types; SCE_OBJECT (3) is one that no generated or real ledger of the corpus showed before. Readers that map only SCE_CONTRACT and a few host error types fail or mislabel this error value when it appears as event data.

entries.title: ScVal Error(Budget, ExceededLimit) from a diagnostic event of a failed Soroban transaction (pubnet history ledger 64558277)
entries.why: stellar-core writes Error(Budget, ExceededLimit) into the diagnostic events of a failed Soroban transaction (topic 1 of the "error" event). Error(Storage, ExceededLimit) has the same ScErrorCode and another ScErrorType: a native conversion that keeps only the code cannot tell which host subsystem failed.

entries.title: ScVal Error(Storage, ExceededLimit) from a diagnostic event of a failed Soroban transaction (testnet history ledger 5521432)
entries.why: stellar-core writes Error(Storage, ExceededLimit) into the diagnostic events of a failed Soroban transaction (topic 1 of the "error" event). Error(Budget, ExceededLimit) has the same ScErrorCode and another ScErrorType: a native conversion that keeps only the code cannot tell which host subsystem failed.

entries.title: InvokeHostFunction whose argument is SCV_MAP with the map absent; the host traps while applying
entries.why: SCVal's map arm is an optional SCMap, and its absent state is valid XDR that no contract can produce. stellar-core admits the transaction and the host refuses the argument while applying (INVOKE_HOST_FUNCTION_TRAPPED), so the absent map sits in a ledger's envelope. Readers that assume SCV_MAP always holds a map dereference nothing.

entries.title: ScVal map with keys Bool(true), U32(1) and I32(1), which collide as native keys
entries.why: The three keys are distinct ScVals in host order, so the map is valid on chain, but they collapse to one or two native key(s) in a language whose maps are keyed by text or by a loosely typed value. A converter must keep all three entries or refuse; silently keeping fewer loses data.

entries.title: ScVal map with keys U32(1), String("1") and Symbol("1"), which collide as native text keys
entries.why: The three keys are distinct ScVals in host order, so the map is valid on chain, but they collapse to one or two native key(s) in a language whose maps are keyed by text or by a loosely typed value. A converter must keep all three entries or refuse; silently keeping fewer loses data.

entries.title: ScVal map whose keys U32(1) and Symbol("1") collide when converted to native keys
entries.why: The two keys are distinct ScVals in host order, so a contract can return or emit this map. Converting it to a native object keyed by text makes both keys "1": a converter that does not refuse silently drops one entry.

entries.title: Contract event whose data is 99 nested vectors, the host maximum
entries.why: The host lets a contract emit a value nested 99 vectors deep (100 fails), so consensus meta carries it: in the event data and in the return value. Readers whose decoder or JSON conversion stops below that depth fail on a valid ledger.

entries.title: Contract event whose data is SCV_TIMEPOINT (arm 7), emitted on a local chain
entries.why: SCV_TIMEPOINT is a valid SCVal arm that contracts rarely emit, so readers' SCVal switches often miss it: a converter that has no case for it drops the event data, renders it as an unknown type, or fails the event. SEP-51 renders it as a decimal string of seconds.

entries.title: ExtendFootprintTtl and RestoreFootprint with muxed transaction and operation sources
entries.why: The Soroban maintenance operations accept M… transaction and operation sources (only InvokeHostFunction forbids them from Protocol 25). The fees and sequence numbers belong to the base accounts. Readers that truncate the muxed source, store only the M form, or fail on a muxed source for these operations misreport or halt.

entries.title: Pubnet ledger 50574257 (protocol 20): a wasm upload whose ContractCodeEntry has ext v0, before cost inputs existed
entries.why: Contract code uploaded under protocol 20 is stored with ContractCodeEntry.ext v0; protocol 21 (CAP-0054) added ext v1 with ContractCodeCostInputs, and entries written before it keep v0 for good. Readers that assume every code entry carries cost inputs, or that only ever saw generated entries (all v1), fail on this real upload.

entries.title: UploadContractWasm creates a ContractCodeEntry whose ext.v1 holds ContractCodeCostInputs
entries.why: From Protocol 21 a created ContractCodeEntry carries ext.v1 with the module's cost inputs. Readers built on pre-21 XDR, or that assume ext v0, fail to decode or drop it.

entries.title: Contract with a no-argument constructor deployed with the v1 host function and v2 authorization
entries.why: A contract with a constructor can be deployed with the old CREATE_CONTRACT host function or the new CREATE_CONTRACT_V2, and authorized with either authorization form; all four combinations run the constructor, which writes storage in the same operation. Readers keyed on one host-function arm miss the others.

entries.title: Contract with a no-argument constructor deployed with the v1 host function and v1 authorization
entries.why: A contract with a constructor can be deployed with the old CREATE_CONTRACT host function or the new CREATE_CONTRACT_V2, and authorized with either authorization form; all four combinations run the constructor, which writes storage in the same operation. Readers keyed on one host-function arm miss the others.

entries.title: Contract with a no-argument constructor deployed with the v2 host function and v1 authorization
entries.why: A contract with a constructor can be deployed with the old CREATE_CONTRACT host function or the new CREATE_CONTRACT_V2, and authorized with either authorization form; all four combinations run the constructor, which writes storage in the same operation. Readers keyed on one host-function arm miss the others.

entries.title: CreateContractV2 with constructor arguments and a constructor that requires authorization
entries.why: Protocol 22's CREATE_CONTRACT_V2 host function carries constructor arguments, and the constructor itself can call require_auth, so the authorization tree has a CREATE_CONTRACT_V2_HOST_FN root with a __constructor sub-invocation. Readers that only know CREATE_CONTRACT cannot decode it.

entries.title: Contract with a no-argument constructor deployed with the v2 host function and v2 authorization
entries.why: A contract with a constructor can be deployed with the old CREATE_CONTRACT host function or the new CREATE_CONTRACT_V2, and authorized with either authorization form; all four combinations run the constructor, which writes storage in the same operation. Readers keyed on one host-function arm miss the others.

entries.title: CREATE_CONTRACT_V2 with a constructor argument; the constructor's event in the same transaction
entries.why: CREATE_CONTRACT_V2 passes constructor arguments, and the constructor runs in the deploying transaction: its storage write and its event appear there, emitted by the new contract. Readers that expect a deployment to carry no events, or that read only CREATE_CONTRACT, miss them.

entries.title: Protocol 30 ledger evicting three persistent contract-data entries to the hot archive
entries.why: Since CAP-62 persistent entries are evicted too: they move to the hot archive and can be restored, so an evicted PERSISTENT key is not a deletion. This ledger's evictedKeys has three TTL keys and three persistent CONTRACT_DATA keys. Readers that treat evictedKeys as deletions, or that expect only temporary entries there, lose restorable state.

entries.title: Temporary entry re-created with the same key on the ledger where its expired predecessor is evicted
entries.why: A temporary entry that expired is re-created under the same key in the ledger that evicts the old one. The meta shows a plain 'created' change. Readers that key state by entry key and process eviction after transactions delete the new entry.

entries.title: Ledger with no transactions that evicts a persistent contract-data entry and its TTL
entries.why: Since Protocol 23 an evicted persistent entry leaves the live state through the ledger's evictedKeys list, with no transaction and no entry change. Readers that only read transaction meta never see the eviction and keep the entry live.

entries.title: Ledger evicting a temporary and a persistent contract entry past their TTL
entries.why: Eviction happens at ledger close with no transaction: the keys of the evicted entries and their TTL entries appear only in LedgerCloseMeta's evicted_keys, temporary entries are deleted and persistent ones move to the hot archive. Readers that track contract state from transaction meta alone keep entries that no longer exist.

entries.title: LedgerCloseMeta whose classic component and non-empty parallel Soroban phase both leave the base fee out
entries.why: ParallelTxsComponent.baseFee is absent in real ledgers only when the Soroban phase is empty. Here it is absent with a Soroban transaction in the phase, alongside a classic component without one: every inclusion fee is then the transaction's own bid, which a reader must take from the results, not from the phase.

entries.title: Generalized transaction set at Protocol 23+: empty classic phase, Soroban phase with one stage and one cluster
entries.why: From Protocol 23 the Soroban phase of a transaction set is v1: execution stages of parallel clusters. Here the classic phase v0 is empty and the Soroban phase has one stage holding one cluster with one transaction. Readers that walk only the v0 phase layout, or that assume the classic phase is non-empty, find no transactions.

entries.title: Three read-only TTL extensions of the same entry in one parallel stage
entries.why: Three transactions extend the TTL of the same read-only entry within one stage of the parallel phase. Readers that apply TTL changes by transaction order in the set, or assume one change per key per ledger, record the wrong final TTL.

entries.title: Persistent entry deleted in one stage and re-created with a lower TTL in another
entries.why: One transaction deletes a persistent entry and another, in a later stage of the same ledger, re-creates it with a lower TTL. Readers that process changes in set order instead of apply order end with the entry deleted or with the wrong TTL.

entries.title: Parallel Soroban phase with several stages and clusters; apply order differs from set order
entries.why: Since Protocol 23 the Soroban phase is a list of execution stages, each a list of clusters of transactions. Results and meta follow apply order, which is not the order of the transaction set. Readers that zip envelopes with results by position attach the wrong result to a transaction.

entries.title: Soroban fee refund applied after all transactions, in post-apply fee processing
entries.why: Since Protocol 23 the Soroban resource-fee refund is applied after the whole transaction set, in TransactionResultMetaV1.postTxApplyFeeProcessing, not inside the transaction's meta. Readers that only read tx meta miss the refund and overstate the fee.

entries.title: Invocation touching an archived entry without listing it in archivedSorobanEntries fails
entries.why: When a transaction's footprint includes an archived entry but archivedSorobanEntries does not index it, the invocation fails with ENTRY_ARCHIVED and nothing is restored. Readers that assume the host restores every archived footprint entry record a restoration that did not happen.

entries.title: Auto-restore of an expired but not yet evicted entry during a read
entries.why: A read-only call touches an expired, not yet evicted persistent entry; the host restores it automatically and the meta shows 'restored' changes although the contract only read. Readers that assume a read changes nothing miss the restoration.

entries.title: Auto-restore then delete of an evicted entry in one operation
entries.why: An evicted entry is restored and deleted in the same operation: the meta shows 'restored' then 'removed' for both the entry and its TTL. Readers that apply changes by key without order lose one of the two.

entries.title: Auto-restore of an evicted entry in the same operation that updates it
entries.why: An InvokeHostFunction call writes to an evicted persistent entry listed in archivedSorobanEntries: the meta shows the entry and its TTL 'restored', then the entry 'updated' to the new value, all in one operation. Readers that expect restore to be a separate operation, or apply only the last change per key, lose the restoration.

entries.title: InvokeHostFunction that restores an archived entry automatically: RESTORED then UPDATED
entries.why: From Protocol 23 a transaction can restore archived entries it lists in archived_soroban_entries; its operation meta shows LEDGER_ENTRY_RESTORED for the entry and its TTL, followed by UPDATED for the write, with no STATE change. Readers that expect every UPDATED to follow a STATE, or that ignore RESTORED, get the entry's history wrong.

entries.title: Pubnet InvokeHostFunction that auto-restores an archived contract code entry (LEDGER_ENTRY_RESTORED)
entries.why: Since Protocol 23 an invocation whose footprint marks an archived entry for restore brings it back in the same operation, and the meta reports it as LEDGER_ENTRY_RESTORED. Here the archived entry is the contract's Wasm, a CONTRACT_CODE entry, restored with its TTL among ordinary state/updated changes; readers that only expect contract data to be restored, or that do not know the restored change type, drop the code entry.

entries.title: Protocol 22 RestoreFootprint whose regenerated lake meta carries `restored` ledger-entry changes
entries.why: LEDGER_ENTRY_RESTORED changes were added by CAP-66 in Protocol 23; a node at Protocol 22 reported a restore as created or updated entries. The lake's object for this Protocol 22 ledger was re-emitted by a Protocol 23 stellar-core, so the restore shows as two `restored` changes (the TTL and the contract data) in TransactionMeta v4, with backfilled fee events. Readers that branch on the ledger's protocol to decide which change types can occur, or that only know created/updated/removed/state, drop or mis-type the restored entries.

entries.title: One InvokeHostFunction restores an archived balance entry and its TTL, then updates it
entries.why: With CAP-66 an invocation can restore archived entries itself: the envelope marks read-write footprint index 1 in archivedSorobanEntries and the operation meta shows LEDGER_ENTRY_RESTORED for the TTL and the contract data, then UPDATED for the same contract data. Readers that do not know the RESTORED change type fail to decode or drop it, and readers that treat restored as created double-count the entry.

entries.title: Manual RestoreFootprint of an entry that was evicted
entries.why: RestoreFootprint emits the same 'restored' changes whether the entry was evicted to the hot archive or only expired in the live state; only the ledger history tells the two apart. Readers that infer eviction from the restore, or require a preceding eviction, get the entry's history wrong.

entries.title: Manual RestoreFootprint of an entry that expired but was not evicted
entries.why: RestoreFootprint emits the same 'restored' changes whether the entry was evicted to the hot archive or only expired in the live state; only the ledger history tells the two apart. Readers that infer eviction from the restore, or require a preceding eviction, get the entry's history wrong.

entries.title: RestoreFootprint whose refundable fee cannot pay the restore's rent fails with INSUFFICIENT_REFUNDABLE_FEE
entries.why: The resource fee of 4000 covers the non-refundable part, so the transaction is admitted, but what is left for refundable charges is less than the rent the restore costs. The operation fails while applying; readers that compute fees from the declared resource fee or expect a refund misreport what E paid.

entries.title: RestoreFootprint of an archived entry with no disk-read bytes declared fails with RESOURCE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED
entries.why: Restoring reads the archived entry from disk, so the transaction must declare at least its size in disk-read bytes. This one declares none; stellar-core finds out only while applying, after the entry was evicted to the hot archive (CAP-0062, CAP-0066). The entry stays archived.

entries.title: SAC transfer (custom asset) to a muxed account argument: event to is the G address, data carries to_muxed_id
entries.why: The transfer's destination argument is an M address (ScAddress::MuxedAccount). The event's to topic is the base G address and the muxed ID moves into the data map as to_muxed_id. Readers that keep the envelope's M form, or expect bare i128 data, get the recipient or the amount wrong.

entries.title: SAC transfer (native asset) to a muxed account argument: event to is the G address, data carries to_muxed_id
entries.why: The transfer's destination argument is an M address (ScAddress::MuxedAccount). The event's to topic is the base G address and the muxed ID moves into the data map as to_muxed_id. Readers that keep the envelope's M form, or expect bare i128 data, get the recipient or the amount wrong.

entries.title: Busy Protocol 27 ledger as a receipt count: 216 transactions, 593 events (249 fee, 227 transfer, 117 mint)
entries.why: A reader that ingests this ledger must end up with exactly 216 transactions, 573 operations and 593 events: 216 fee charges before all transactions plus 33 refunds after them, 227 transfers and 117 mints. The entry pins the whole-ledger counts rather than one transaction, so readers that drop failed transactions' fee events, skip refunds, double-count events or lose classic events show up as a count mismatch.

entries.title: Classic events whose from or to is a liquidity pool or a claimable balance address
entries.why: From Protocol 23 classic operations emit transfer events, and for pool deposits and claimable balances one side of the transfer is an L or B address, not an account. Readers that assume every event address is a G or C address fail to decode, drop or misattribute these movements.

entries.title: Custom contract events (exposure_synced) next to the native contract's fee events in the same transactions
entries.why: A transaction's events mix the native asset contract's transaction-level fee events with a protocol contract's own event (exposure_synced, two symbol topics and a vector of i128). Readers that treat every contract event as a token movement, or every event of a fee-paying transaction as a fee, invent movements from the custom event; readers that only keep token-shaped events must still keep the fee events.

entries.title: Fee events: charge before all transactions, negative refund after them; native approve to an account
entries.why: Since Protocol 23 (CAP-67) the native asset contract emits transaction-level fee events: one with stage BEFORE_ALL_TXS that charges the full fee, and for a Soroban transaction one with stage AFTER_ALL_TXS whose amount is negative, the refund. Readers that treat every fee event as a charge, that take the absolute value, or that read only operation events, report the wrong fee or none. The focus is a native-asset approve, which moves no value and leaves the fee events as the only movements.

entries.title: Fee events: charge before all transactions, negative refund after them; native approve to the native contract itself
entries.why: Since Protocol 23 (CAP-67) the native asset contract emits transaction-level fee events: one with stage BEFORE_ALL_TXS that charges the full fee, and for a Soroban transaction one with stage AFTER_ALL_TXS whose amount is negative, the refund. Readers that treat every fee event as a charge, that take the absolute value, or that read only operation events, report the wrong fee or none. The focus is a native-asset approve, which moves no value and leaves the fee events as the only movements.

entries.title: Transfer event shaped like a Stellar Asset Contract event, from a contract that is not that asset's
entries.why: Any contract can emit an event with topics [transfer, from, to, "USD:G…"]. Only the event's contractID says whose token it is; here it is the test emitter, not USD's contract, and no balance changes. A reader that keys movements on the event's asset string credits the victim with USD it never received.

entries.title: Custom-token mint in the legacy layout [mint, admin, to]: three topics, the second is the token itself
entries.why: A custom token (not a Stellar Asset Contract) emits mint with the pre-CAP-67 SEP-41 layout [mint, admin, to], three topics like the CAP-67 SAC form [mint, to, asset] but in another order. Readers that apply the SAC layout to every three-topic mint credit the admin (here the token contract itself) and read the recipient as the asset.

entries.title: Custom-token mint in the legacy layout [mint, admin, to] after a BLND deposit (no fee bump)
entries.why: A second contract with the pre-CAP-67 SEP-41 mint layout [mint, admin, to] in a plain (not fee-bumped) transaction: GBY2Q24L… deposits BLND and the contract CASYAKK3… mints its own token to it, naming itself as admin. Readers that apply the SAC three-topic layout to every mint credit the contract and lose the recipient.

entries.title: Classic payment event carrying a MEMO_ID as to_muxed_id u64
entries.why: For a payment to an unmuxed account stellar-core copies a MEMO_ID into the event's to_muxed_id as a u64, the same type a muxed destination produces. The value is the sender's memo, not a muxed account ID, so a reader that builds an M address from it invents a destination.

entries.title: Classic payment event carrying a MEMO_RETURN as to_muxed_id bytes
entries.why: stellar-core copies a MEMO_RETURN into the event's to_muxed_id as 32 bytes, exactly as it copies a MEMO_HASH, so the event alone cannot tell the two memo types apart. Readers must take the memo type from the envelope and never read the bytes as a key.

entries.title: Payment whose 28-byte MEMO_TEXT is the start of a G address, copied into the event
entries.why: The memo is the first 28 characters of a real account's G address and becomes the event's to_muxed_id string. It is sender-chosen text; readers that treat routing text as an address, or complete it to one, invent a participant.

entries.title: Eleven Stellar Asset Contract mint events in one transaction, one trustline credited once with their sum
entries.why: One harvest call makes the KALE Stellar Asset Contract mint eleven times to the same account: eleven CAP-67 mint events with eleven different amounts, but a single trustline update whose delta is their sum (84208029). Readers that keep one movement per transaction or per operation, that de-duplicate events with the same topics, or that reconcile movements against the one balance change, lose or merge mints.

entries.title: Stellar Asset Contract mint inside a contract call: three-topic CAP-67 event, recipient's trustline credited
entries.why: The KALE Stellar Asset Contract mints to an account from inside another contract's harvest call, so the envelope names no mint and no asset: only the three-topic event [mint, to, asset] and the recipient's trustline change show it. Readers that derive balance effects only from classic operations, or that expect the pre-CAP-67 four-topic layout with an admin, drop the credit.

entries.title: Stellar Asset Contract transfer to a muxed account: event names the G address and carries the ID
entries.why: The contract call's destination argument is a muxed M address, but the transfer event's to topic is the base G address and the muxed ID moves into the data map as to_muxed_id. Readers that expect a bare i128 drop or zero the amount, and readers that take the destination from the envelope keep an M address the ledger never stores.

entries.title: SAC transfer to a muxed account with ID 8719886936707710911, on both passphrases
entries.why: A Stellar Asset Contract transfer to an M address credits the base account: the event's to topic is the G address and the muxed ID travels in a data map as to_muxed_id. Readers that expect plain i128 data, store the M form as the account, or read the ID as a float64 misreport the transfer.

entries.title: SEP-41 burn and approve events whose data is a map with symbol keys
entries.why: SEP-41 allows burn data {amount} and approve data {amount, live_until_ledger} as maps instead of an i128 and a vector. Readers that expect only the bare forms drop or misparse these events.

entries.title: Classic payment event whose data is a bare i128, with no to_muxed_id key
entries.why: When the destination is not muxed and the transaction has no memo, the transfer event's data is a bare i128, not a map. Readers that expect the map form fail to read the amount, and readers that turn the missing key into muxed ID 0 invent routing that is not there.

entries.title: Classic payment event carrying the 32-byte MEMO_HASH as to_muxed_id bytes
entries.why: For a payment to an unmuxed account, stellar-core copies a MEMO_HASH into the event's to_muxed_id as 32 bytes. The bytes are sender-chosen and have the length of an ed25519 key, so readers that pad, truncate or decode them as a muxed ID or an address invent a destination.

entries.title: Issuer payment emitted as a three-topic mint event carrying the text memo as to_muxed_id
entries.why: A payment whose operation source is the asset issuer is emitted as a mint event [mint, to, asset] with three topics, and the transaction's text memo is copied into its to_muxed_id. Readers that look for to_muxed_id only on transfer events, or that turn the memo text into a muxed ID, get the routing wrong.

entries.title: Five classic payments whose transfer events carry the text memo as to_muxed_id
entries.why: For a payment to an unmuxed account, stellar-core copies the transaction's text memo into the event's to_muxed_id as a string. It is sender-chosen text, not a muxed ID: readers that turn it into a muxed ID (0, or a parsed number) or into an M address fabricate a muxed destination.

entries.title: Payment with a non-UTF-8 MEMO_TEXT copied into the event's to_muxed_id string
entries.why: stellar-core checks only the 28-byte limit of a text memo, so bytes ff fe 00 c3 28 ed a0 80 41 are accepted and copied into the classic event as an SCV_STRING. Readers that decode memo or event strings as UTF-8 replace or drop bytes, or fail.

entries.title: Payment to a muxed destination in a transaction with a text memo: the event carries the muxed ID
entries.why: The transaction has a text memo, yet the payment to the M destination carries its muxed ID as to_muxed_id: the muxed ID takes precedence over the memo. The same transaction's other operation carries the memo text instead, so a reader cannot take routing from the transaction; it must read each event.

entries.title: Custom token transfer event with three topics and to_muxed_id explicitly Void
entries.why: A contract that is not the Stellar Asset Contract emits a SEP-41 transfer event whose data map has to_muxed_id set to Void, a value stellar-core never emits for classic events. Readers that accept only u64, bytes or string there drop the whole event, and the movement goes missing.

entries.title: Custom-token transfer event whose to_muxed_id is 4 bytes
entries.why: CAP-0067 allows to_muxed_id as u64, bytes or string. Bytes are not a fixed length: here 4. A reader that pads or truncates them to 32 bytes reports a different routing ID; the event comes from a custom contract, so nothing moves on the ledger.

entries.title: Custom-token transfer event whose to_muxed_id is 40 bytes
entries.why: Bytes longer than a 32-byte hash: a reader that truncates them to 32 bytes reports a different routing ID. The event comes from a custom contract, so nothing moves on the ledger.

entries.title: Custom-token transfer event whose to_muxed_id is an I32, a type CAP-0067 does not allow
entries.why: A custom contract can put any value in to_muxed_id. I32(5) is none of u64, bytes or string, so a reader must treat the routing ID as non-conforming rather than read it as the number 5 or fail.

entries.title: Transfer event in the token-event layout whose to topic is a symbol, not an address
entries.why: A contract can publish any topics. Here the third topic of a `[transfer, from, to]` event is the symbol `not_an_address`. A reader that converts the `to` topic into an address or muxed address must return an error and keep reading; one that panics, halts or books a transfer to some address is wrong. Nothing moves and only the source account changes.

entries.title: Protocol 23 upgrade creates the CONFIG_SETTING_SCP_TIMING entry (5000 ms target close time)
entries.why: CAP-70 moved the ledger close-time target and SCP timeouts into a network configuration setting. The setting does not exist before Protocol 23: the upgrade ledger creates it as one of nine upgrade changes, with a 5000 ms target close time and 1000 ms nomination and ballot timeouts. Readers that only know the Protocol 20-22 config-setting arms cannot decode the upgrade changes of this ledger, and readers that ignore upgrade changes never learn the network's timing.

entries.title: Upgrade ledger of a fresh chain creating CONFIG_SETTING_SCP_TIMING among the other settings
entries.why: CAP-0070 adds the SCP timing setting, created by the version upgrade that crosses Protocol 23 with the other configuration settings. A reader built on definitions without CONFIG_SETTING_SCP_TIMING cannot decode the upgrade ledger of any chain that crosses 23.
